lesson.grammar_point: be used to and get used to for describing progress

listenings.text: Almost every executive I work with has the same moment. After three or four months, they come to a session and say: I've stopped improving. And I understand the feeling. At the beginning, progress is easy to see. You learn fifty words, you use them the next day. Then the easy progress is over, and what is left is harder to notice: speed, confidence, the words that come without thinking. So you plateau, or you think you do. Most of the time the feeling is wrong. So I give them three tips. First, record yourself once a month, and compare. The difference you cannot feel, you can hear. Second, do one thing every week that is outside your comfort zone. And third, set one stretch goal at a time. Not five. One.

When I went to my first conferences in English, I used to hide. Really. I used to sit at the back of the room, check my phone at every coffee break, and leave before the dinner, because the dinner was where people actually talked. That was about ten years ago, at a bank in Mexico City. Today I'm used to starting conversations with strangers, and I'm used to presenting numbers on a panel. That took a few years. I'm still getting used to jokes in English, and to some very fast accents. But here's my advice. Don't wait until you feel ready. Nobody feels ready. You get used to it by doing it, one conversation at a time.

paras: Ask an adult learner how much their English has improved in the last two months, and the answer is usually not much. Ask the teacher, or listen to a recording from the first week, and the answer is very different. Adults are bad at measuring their own progress, and there is a simple reason: the most important changes are the ones you stop noticing.

In the first weeks, progress is easy to see. New words, new structures, a first presentation that works. Then something strange happens. The learner seems to plateau. The words are still there, but the feeling of moving forward disappears. This is the moment when many people give up, or decide that a course is not working.

Most of the time, the plateau is an illusion. What has changed is not the amount of English, but the way it comes out. Things that needed planning in lesson five now come as muscle memory: the opener, the pause after a number, the question tag at the bar. People are used to hearing progress as more. Real progress at this stage is easier, and easier is hard to feel from the inside.

That is why professionals track progress with something outside their own head. A rubric turns a feeling into a score. A recording from one month ago shows a blind spot that nobody could describe to you. And a regular self-assessment, done honestly, shows which tasks have moved out of the danger area and into your comfort zone.

A milestone is the right moment to do all three. Look back, measure, and then choose one stretch goal for the next block: something difficult but possible, a goal that lets you build on what you already have. Not five goals. One.
